context:
FernPass is a fictional shared-workspace operator deduplicating business customer accounts. An entity is a contracting legal organization in a particular registration jurisdiction; shared accountants and franchise names do not establish identity. The implementation runs 46 ordered rules. A verified jurisdiction-scoped registration identifier can accept a pair early; a later rule vetoes conflicting active tax identifiers. Missing identifiers are encoded as empty strings. Some rules add scores, some decide immediately, and three rely on source priority. Engineers cannot currently say whether an early acceptance bypasses the veto.

Management wants a readable decision table, not a new matching model. There are 85,000 historical candidate pairs with recorded rule traces and decisions, but only 160 independently adjudicated identity judgments from a single source pair. Historical agreement is required for an initial no-behavior-change refactor; it is not a guarantee that those decisions are correct. Compliance prohibits production changes until a reviewer signs off on conflict semantics. An offline replay environment can retain versioned inputs and traces. The candidate generator and normalization code are nominally unchanged but have no pinned artifact hashes yet.

Propose how to specify and test this bounded refactor. Compare retaining the ordered policy to a decision-table alternative, including precedence, vetoes, missingness, abstention and overlap witnesses. Separate behavioral equivalence from identity accuracy. Explain test scope, non-exhaustiveness, escalation conditions, versioned inputs and what evidence would justify a later intentional policy change rather than silently folding it into the refactor.
title: FernPass eligibility policy refactor
